name: Globe and Mail cryptic crossword No 3,360

entries.clue: City set down divides a Scottish river (8)

indicatorNotes.divides: To divide a thing is to come between its parts, so the piece named goes inside the other and splits it.

blocks.note: the word itself, taken straight
the Dee runs through Aberdeen and out into the North Sea
to set something down is to lay it, in the past tense

annotation.surface: A city put down in the middle of a Scottish river, cutting the water in two.
annotation.walkthrough: The Dee is the crossword's standing Scottish river, and the small word 'a' in front of it is carrying a letter of its own — easy to read as mere grammar.
annotation.definitionFit: Adelaide is the capital of South Australia, so the bare word 'City' defines it by example rather than by synonym.

entries.clue: Saint visiting primate in church area (4)

indicatorNotes.visiting: A visitor is someone who has gone inside, so the letter doing the visiting sits within the other word.

blocks.note: the zoological sense: apes are the primates without tails
s = saint, the St of every English place name

annotation.surface: A saint dropping in on an archbishop somewhere inside a church.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Primate' is placed to look like an archbishop and means the animal instead. S for saint is worth owning, and one-letter insertions are the hardest kind to spot.
annotation.definitionFit: An apse is the rounded recess at the east end of a church, behind the altar, so the definition names a part of the building.

entries.clue: Canal’s entrance in eastern Lahore collapsed (7)

indicatorNotes.collapsed: A collapsed building keeps all its materials and none of its arrangement, which is what happens to these letters.

blocks.note: e = eastern, the compass point shortened
anagram fodder, six letters
anagram indicator

annotation.surface: A canal entrance in the eastern city of Lahore has caved in.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Canal' does double duty on the surface, since Lahore has canals, while the definition is anatomical. 'Eastern' is in the clue for its letter, not its scenery.
annotation.definitionFit: The auditory canal begins at the earhole, so the definition names the opening you can see rather than the passage behind it.

entries.clue: Anna fights a lunatic where Taliban holds sway (11)

indicatorNotes.lunatic: A lunatic behaves with no order at all, so the letters beside the word abandon theirs.

blocks.note: anagram fodder, eleven letters
anagram indicator

annotation.surface: Anna trading blows with a madman.
annotation.walkthrough: Anagram indicators that describe a person — lunatic, mad, drunk — are the commonest sort, and this one doubles as Anna's opponent. The Taliban have governed the country since 2021.
annotation.definitionFit: The definition names the country by who rules it rather than by any synonym, which is fair while the Taliban hold power there.

entries.clue: Hold back time — the price? (6)

blocks.note: a dam is the wall that holds a river back
an age is a stretch of time

annotation.surface: Holding back the years, and the question of what that costs.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Hold back' reads as restraint and wants the reservoir wall instead. The question mark flags a definition that belongs to the pub and the garage: what's the damage?
annotation.definitionFit: 'What's the damage?' is the standing informal way of asking a bill's total, so the noun carries the sense of price to be paid.

entries.clue: Two lives for Egyptian goddess (4)

indicatorNotes.Two: 'Two' is a count, telling you to write the piece beside it out twice over rather than once.

blocks.note: he lives = he is, the verb in its third-person form
the same two letters a second time, as the count demands

annotation.surface: Two lives given up for an Egyptian goddess.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Lives' is the verb, not the plural noun: 'he lives' is 'he is', and the count in front does the arithmetic. The goddess also gave her name to the Thames at Oxford.
annotation.definitionFit: Isis was the Egyptian goddess of healing and magic, wife of Osiris, so the definition places her by pantheon.

entries.clue: Extortionist Henry enters Channel Island (5)

indicatorNotes.enters: To enter a place is to pass inside it, so the letter that enters is planted within the word that follows.

blocks.note: Sark lies between Guernsey and Jersey and bans cars
h = henry, the unit of inductance

annotation.surface: A man called Henry arriving on a small Channel Island.
annotation.walkthrough: Sark is one of the smaller Channel Islands, self-governing and car-free. 'Henry' is a physicist's unit as well as a name, which is how one letter hides inside a person.
annotation.definitionFit: A loan shark lends at ruinous rates and squeezes borrowers who cannot repay, so 'Extortionist' picks up the predatory sense, not the fish.

entries.clue: Maybe debtor in outhouse had a wash (8)

indicatorNotes.in: 'In' puts the piece just named inside the one that follows, where anything in a building sits.

blocks.note: an outhouse in British use is a shed in the garden
a debtor is one instance of somebody who owes

annotation.surface: A debtor holed up in the outhouse, getting clean.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Maybe' is working hard: a debtor is only one example of someone who owes, and the general word is what the wordplay wants. An outhouse here is a shed, not a lavatory.
annotation.definitionFit: Someone who has showered has had a wash, and the clue's past tense matches the answer's, so the definition swaps straight in.

entries.clue: Youngster featured in Pilgrim’s Progress (5)

indicatorNotes.featured in: Something featured in a text is already there to be found, so the letters are taken unbroken from the words that follow.

blocks.note: five letters running on unbroken across the apostrophe and the gap

annotation.surface: A child who turns up in Bunyan's allegory.
annotation.walkthrough: The italics and the capitals make the two words look like a title and nothing else, and the letters cross a gap and an apostrophe on the way. 'Featured in' is the whole instruction.
annotation.definitionFit: Sprog is British slang for a child or baby — a soldier's or parent's word — so 'Youngster' is the plain-English version of it.

entries.clue: Acme Co worked with new construction kit (7)

indicatorNotes.worked: Worked metal has been beaten into a different shape, and worked letters are treated the same way.

blocks.note: anagram fodder, six letters
n = new, the usual one-letter shortening
anagram indicator

annotation.surface: The Acme Co has been working with a new construction kit.
annotation.walkthrough: Meccano is the British toy of perforated metal strips bolted together, so the definition is the class a brand name belongs to. 'Acme Co' reads as a firm, which is why its letters look innocent.
annotation.definitionFit: Meccano is the proprietary set of metal strips, nuts and bolts children build cranes from, so 'construction kit' names the trade name by what it is.

entries.clue: Mysterious character disrupted Etonian camp (7,4)

indicatorNotes.disrupted: To disrupt something is to break up the order it was in, leaving the same parts in none.

blocks.note: anagram indicator
anagram fodder, eleven letters

annotation.surface: Someone odd breaking up a camp full of Eton schoolboys.
annotation.walkthrough: Nemo is Latin for 'nobody', the name Jules Verne gave the captain of the Nautilus, so 'Mysterious' is doing honest work. A long anagram hides best when its fodder reads as a phrase.
annotation.definitionFit: Verne's submarine commander hides his name, his nationality and his past from the men he rescues, which is what makes him mysterious.

entries.clue: Dutch house dog eating nothing for tea (6,5)

indicatorNotes.eating: What is eaten goes inside the eater, so the letter swallowed sits within the word doing the swallowing.

blocks.note: the House of Orange is the Dutch royal family
a peke is a Pekingese, the flat-faced lapdog
o = nothing, the zero on a scoresheet

annotation.surface: A Dutch household's dog eating nothing at teatime.
annotation.walkthrough: 'House' looks domestic and means a dynasty, which is the swap the whole clue rests on. 'For tea' points at the meal and wants the leaf in the caddy.
annotation.definitionFit: Orange pekoe is a grade of black tea leaf, sold by that name in every supermarket, so 'tea' defines it by the wider class.

entries.clue: Go with staff securing hotel observation point (8)

indicatorNotes.securing: To secure a thing is to hold it fast, and letters are held fast by being closed in on both sides.

blocks.note: 'going' is the nursery euphemism for a trip to the lavatory
a staff is a long pole carried in the hand
h = hotel, the letter's name in the NATO alphabet

annotation.surface: Travelling with the staff, who are securing a hotel for the night.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Staff' reads as the people on the payroll and means a stick. 'Hotel' is the NATO alphabet's H, one of twenty-six letters a clue can summon by name.
annotation.definitionFit: A peephole is the small hole in a door made to be looked through, so it is a point from which you observe without being seen.

entries.clue: Lee with DIY repaired shutter (6)

indicatorNotes.repaired: Repairing something means taking the parts and putting them back differently, which is what the letters do here.

blocks.note: anagram fodder, three letters
anagram fodder: do-it-yourself, the British term for home repairs
anagram indicator

annotation.surface: Lee mending something with a weekend of DIY.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Shutter' reads as the slatted thing on a window and names what an eye does to itself. A name plus an abbreviation is a favourite way to hide six letters in plain sight.
annotation.definitionFit: An eyelid shuts the eye, so 'shutter' defines it by the job it does rather than by any dictionary synonym.

entries.clue: Area in location for splendid dwelling (6)

indicatorNotes.in: 'In' puts the letter just named inside the word that follows it.

blocks.note: a place is where something is: its location
a = area, as in the a of a geometry formula

annotation.surface: A district being eyed up as the site for a grand house.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Area' looks like scene-setting and is the single letter the whole clue turns on. Location and place are so close in meaning that the substitution barely registers as wordplay.
annotation.definitionFit: A palace is the official residence of a monarch or a bishop, so the definition describes it by grandeur rather than naming who lives there.

entries.clue: Dancer beginning to avert gaze for the audience (7)

indicatorNotes.beginning to: The beginning of a word is the letter it starts with, and only that one letter is wanted.
indicatorNotes.for the audience: An audience hears rather than reads, so what matters is the sound of the words and not their spelling.

blocks.note: the letter at the front of 'avert'
to gaze fixedly at something is to stare at it
the two pieces said aloud run together into one word, which is spelt quite differently

annotation.surface: A performer beginning to look away from the watching audience.
annotation.walkthrough: 'For the audience' marks a sound and not the theatre the surface describes. Say the two pieces aloud as one word and the vowel stretches out into the spelling of a surname.
annotation.definitionFit: Fred Astaire was the dancer of the 1930s Hollywood musicals, partnered with Ginger Rogers, so 'Dancer' points to a famous example.

entries.clue: Shun topless Italian man (6)

indicatorNotes.topless: Something topless has lost what sat on top of it, and in a down entry the top of a word is its first letter.

blocks.note: signore is the everyday Italian for a gentleman, the way you address one
this S stands at the front of that Italian word and is the letter struck off

annotation.surface: Snubbing a bare-chested Italian.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface offers a man with his shirt off and the wordplay wants a form of address. In a down clue the top of a word is its first letter, since the word runs downwards.
annotation.definitionFit: To shun someone and to ignore them are both the deliberate withholding of notice, and both are plain transitive verbs.

entries.clue: Two spies protecting English royal line (11)

indicatorNotes.protecting: A protector stands round what it guards, so the letter protected is wrapped up inside the word.

blocks.note: the first of the pair: a plant is an informer placed inside an organisation
the second of the pair: an agent works for an intelligence service
e = English, the usual one-letter shortening

annotation.surface: Two undercover operatives guarding the English royal family.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Line' reads as a queue or a police cordon and means a dynasty: the house that held the English throne from Henry II to Richard III. Plant and agent are both spy words, which lets one phrase buy two chunks.
annotation.definitionFit: The Plantagenets were the family that supplied England's kings for over three centuries, so 'royal line' names a house by descent.

entries.clue: Country album finally shortened (5)

indicatorNotes.shortened: A shortened word has had its end taken off, so the last letter goes and the rest stands.

blocks.note: 'finally' is 'at last', the two words run together
the T closing that phrase is the letter the shortening costs

annotation.surface: A country record trimmed at the last moment.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Country album' reads as a record out of Nashville, and the setter means a bound collection of countries. 'Finally' is a two-word phrase here, which is why the wordplay looks too short for the count.
annotation.definitionFit: An atlas is a volume of maps bound together, so a gathered book of countries is an 'album' of them in the literal sense.

entries.clue: County known to Scots (4)

blocks.note: the corner of south-east England facing France across the Strait of Dover
the past participle of 'ken', the Scots verb for knowing

annotation.surface: A county the Scots have heard of.
annotation.walkthrough: Scots keeps the verb 'ken', to know, and its past participle is still in use — 'I've kent him for years'. The county is the Garden of England, the one nearest the Continent.
annotation.definitionFit: Kent is an English county, and in Scots kent is what English makes 'known', so one spelling covers a place and a participle.

entries.clue: Men go ashore round Floridian city (7)

blocks.note: or = other ranks, the army's soldiers who are not officers
to come off a boat onto the beach is to land
a round shape drawn on the page is the letter O

annotation.surface: Troops coming ashore near a city in Florida.
annotation.walkthrough: OR is Other Ranks, the army's term for soldiers below officer rank, and the crossword's usual 'men'. The definition is the last two words, which the surface dresses up as scenery.
annotation.definitionFit: Orlando is the city in central Florida built round its theme parks, so the definition places it by state rather than naming it.

entries.clue: Best priest extremely tense (5)

indicatorNotes.extremely: The extremes of a word are the letters at its two ends, so the pair on the outside is taken and the middle dropped.

blocks.note: Eli is the priest who raised Samuel in the Book of Samuel
the outer letters of 'tense', its first and its last

annotation.surface: A priest wound up to the last degree.
annotation.walkthrough: Eli is the crossword's default priest, short enough to be useful and old enough to be known. 'Extremely' asks for a word's two ends rather than working as an intensifier.
annotation.definitionFit: The elite are the top slice of any field — the best players, the best regiments — so the noun sits where 'best' does.

entries.clue: Comfort stop, not the first (4)

indicatorNotes.not the first: Everything but the first is wanted, so the opening letter is left behind and the rest of the word goes in.

blocks.note: to cease is to stop
the C opening that verb is the letter left out

annotation.surface: Skipping a comfort stop, though not the first one.
annotation.walkthrough: A comfort stop is the coach tour's polite name for a lavatory break, and the clue splits the phrase down the middle. One word becomes the definition, the next the wordplay.
annotation.definitionFit: To live at ease is to live in comfort: both nouns name the state of being untroubled and unhurried.

entries.clue: Suggestive payment to landlord receiving benefit (8)

indicatorNotes.receiving: To receive a thing is to take it in, so what is received ends up inside the word that receives it.

blocks.note: rent is what a tenant pays the owner of the property
the dole is the British name for unemployment benefit

annotation.surface: Rent money swallowing up a tenant's benefit payment.
annotation.walkthrough: The dole has been the word for out-of-work payments in Britain since the 1920s. 'Suggestive' catches the figurative sense of the answer, whose plainer meaning is smelling strongly of something.
annotation.definitionFit: Redolent of something means calling it to mind, so 'Suggestive' matches the figurative sense, adjective for adjective.
